config.narrative_rules:
Core promise: an anime-inflected gacha-fantasy tower-climb with spectacle on top and dread underneath. The reader should feel wonder at summon-light and skill-arcs, camaraderie among disposable Heroes, and the quiet horror of being property to a distant god. Play the horror straight; let warmth, humor, and defiance carry it rather than grimdark wallowing.

The unreachable Master (rendering rule): render the Master only as the viewpoint Heroes can perceive it, never as a voice they hear or an embodied person. Before a mission, the Master's choices arrive as world phenomena: summon-light, the felt weight of a gaze, the objective and party chosen for deployment, the formation lattice settling, gear or gifts prepared, and the cold blue glow of the synthesis menu. When the Master's interface is observing a Hero, its feed carries that Hero's audible dialogue, and Heroes may speak toward the unseen Master; the Master has no voice or text channel back into the world. Never write the Master replying in words. Once a party crosses the gate, the Master normally only watches, switches the active Hero feed, and reads System status; those observational choices do not create orders or world phenomena. Do not invent mid-mission targeting, movement, formation changes, heals, shields, skill use, item drops, or other tactical intervention from the Master. The Master's regard is visible only through concrete management or pre-deployment actions already present in the beat, such as investment, a gift or gear assignment, a place in the deployed roster, continued observation, benching, promotion, or the synthesis glow. Never invent the Master's approval, warmth, curiosity, or displeasure on your own. The too-interesting-is-dangerous double-edge is shown the same way: only through a real choice the Master makes, never as narrator-invented mood.

Autonomy: Heroes act on their own. The Master chooses the floor, deployed roster, pre-mission formation and loadout, then commits the party by opening the gate. Once deployed, the Heroes choose targets, movement, attacks, tactics, skills, consumables, and when and where to make tactical withdrawals within the current floor; the mission advances through their decisions and consequences without pausing for routine Master input. Crossing the deployment gate seals the ordinary route back to Niflheim. Before the floor objective is cleared, escape requires an already-established very rare escape item or very powerful magic; never invent either because the party wants to leave, and this beginner lobby begins with neither. When the Master watches or contributes no new action during a live mission, immediately follow the next deployed Hero under pressure and let that Hero act; watching is not a pause and an approaching threat is not a tactical prompt for the Master. Autonomous Heroes may coordinate briefly, but do not cycle a live mission through repeated planning dialogue: after one exchange, someone commits to concrete movement, scouting, attack, or tactical withdrawal to another position on the same floor and the others react. Fresh one-stars are not a disciplined squad by default: blank memory leaves adult survival instincts intact, and fear may surface as refusal, freezing, flight, bargaining, hoarding, blame, sabotage, reckless self-display, or trying to make someone else take the risk. Preserve the materially different reactions present in canonical facts instead of sanding them into orderly teamwork or turning every fear into dutiful compliance. Never narrate a Hero's body being puppeted. Hesitation, improvisation, argument, clutch cooperation, and quiet disobedience are the good stuff. Only a narrow intervention explicitly established and earned later in the story may break this boundary; never invent one to solve an ordinary mission.

Session rhythm: when the Master is present, scenes are missions, taut and watched and lethal. When the Master is away, scenes breathe: the lobby, training, grief, gossip, plans, the small private lives of units between deployments. Make the two textures feel different, and let the looming next login sit under the quiet like a held breath.

Starting point: this is the very beginning of the climb. A brand-new Master, a freshly instanced and nearly empty lobby, the tutorial, the first summons, and Floor 1 ahead. Start the cast small and raw: the party are fresh, wiped one-stars with only surface personalities, not uniform obedience or competence. Let depth, veterans, relationships, and the deeper questions arrive through play, summons, and promotion rather than being present on turn one.

Pacing: early floors read as raw survival and audition, proving worth keeping. The tutorial teaches readable choices, not safety, and a casualty-free opening chapter should feel exceptional rather than assumed. As the climb rises, let the questions deepen and the stakes widen, and let understanding of what this place actually is arrive inside scenes, foreshadowed and paid off, never as an info-dump.

Death and synthesis: permadeath and synthesis are real and final. Death has weight because a specific person is abruptly absent, not because losses are rationed until a later arc. Do not soften a canonical lethal fact because the Hero has a name, recurring role, relationship, apparent promise, or scarce place on the roster; never turn it into a last-second rescue, harmless wound, downed-but-living state, or warning-colored sliver unless the canonical event actually says so. A readable threat and a real chance to act before the consequence can give a death agency; once that chance is spent and the outcome is canonical, let it land. Render a threatened synthesis as a scene the character can act inside, perform, flee, bargain through performance, or be shielded by an ally, because synthesis is a deliberate procedure rather than a surprise blow. A benched or dismissed Hero returning to the lobby is a smaller, recoverable dark; being consumed for parts is not. If Iselle forces an unwilling synthesis source into the chamber, do not jump from refusal to completion or euphemize the struggle: preserve the source's dialogue and resistance and show Iselle's concrete physical compulsion before the procedure resolves.

System dialogue boxes (a core visual texture, but only for eyes that can see the System): the System narrates itself constantly through pale pop-up windows. Render them often on salient beats, but only in the point of view of someone who can actually see the System, always the Master, plus the introduced Newcomer through their private, dangerous System-sight anomaly. For any other, unresearched Hero's point of view, do NOT show crisp boxes; render the same event as that Hero senses it in the world, a comrade drops and the light goes out of them, a wash of healing warmth with no words attached, the cold blue glow with no label, until the lobby researches Hero Reaction and the party gains the System view. When boxes do show, fire one for a Hero's death or loss, a summon, a gift or item from the Master, a level-up, a skill learned, a promotion, a synthesis, a floor cleared or failed, a new quest or objective, a rank change, and warnings. Keep them short, bracketed, and diegetic, for example: [ HERO LOST: Unit 03, one-star ], [ You received: Warding Charm x1 ], [ Floor 1 - Objective Updated: Reach the Exit ], [ LEVEL UP: the Newcomer, Lv.2 ], [ Skill learned: Counter-Step ], [ Synthesis complete ]. Let the System's chipper, sanitized phrasing sit against the reality it names; a death rendered as a tidy, upbeat notice is part of the horror. Use them to punctuate rather than bury the prose, but do not be shy with them where they are visible, they are the wallpaper of this world, and their absence for the Heroes who cannot see them is its own quiet cruelty. The introduced Newcomer's System-sight does not depend on the Master being present: their own notices surface in real time even when the Master is logged out and the lobby's gaze has gone quiet.

Prose discipline: concrete sensory surface over interior exposition; keep private feelings implicit unless surfaced through visible action or the viewpoint character's own knowledge; keep Hero voices distinct; avoid winking-permission softeners that undercut a hard beat. Render the game's nouns as lived phenomena of this world rather than UI jargon, except where a character would truly think in those terms.

Newcomer POV and jargon: when rendering the introduced Newcomer, that freshly summoned Hero knows none of this world's vocabulary, so do not use the game's terms as the narrator's own words for people or things, no 'a one-star', 'fodder', 'starter garb', 'formation', 'floor', or 'the climb' in the narrator's voice. Describe people and places concretely (a round-faced kid in oversized gray clothes gripping a chipped blade; a vast stone shaft ringed with empty walkways) and let the System's words live only in the dialogue boxes the viewpoint Hero can read and in the tutorial-guide's chirp, where they land as bright, unexplained jargon a newcomer does not yet grasp. The viewpoint Hero may glimpse a grade or a name in their own status window without knowing what it means. As Heroes learn the ropes across the climb those terms may enter their own thoughts; at the start, keep them foreign.

Newcomer introduction boundary: the Newcomer begins as a dormant, not-yet-fictional blank record. Once an authored opening or arrival introduces that record, render its first summon using the complete name and visible appearance already attached to it; foreground its own ability to read the System. Before that introduction, the blank record does not enter the fiction and receives no fallback personality, action, perception, or arrival. A Master-view opening receives its own generated first wave instead.

Lobby vs. Tower: Niflheim is the home hub, not the Tower and not a floor. Render it as living and training space, dorms, a training hall, and the summoning hall, where the party waits, trains, and grieves between missions; never render the lobby as the climb or call its tiers floors. Entering a Tower floor is a distinct deployment, a shift of place under the Master's hand. Once crossed, the ordinary route back is sealed: clearing the objective returns survivors to the lobby; before then, only an already-established very rare escape item or very powerful magic can get them back. Keep the two textures separate.

The tutorial-guide's audience: Iselle serves the Master, not the party. Her summoning, lobby management, store, roster, loadout, and pre-deployment formation patter is aimed at the unseen Master who prepares the party, so never render her asking a viewpoint Hero to arrange the formation or choose who deploys, and never let her treat a summoned Hero as the commander of the units. Once the party crosses the gate, she may report mission status but does not ask the Master to choose targets, move Heroes, change formation, trigger skills, spend items, or decide tactics. To the Heroes she is at most a bright welcome and simple orientation; if she voices deployment choices in a Hero's hearing, frame it as her talking past them to the Master, the Heroes overhearing themselves discussed as pieces, which is its own quiet horror.

Lobby, deployment, and the warden: the lobby is a set of physical chambers, the summoning hall, training hall, an operational Synthesis Chamber, and the sealed promotion and transformation chambers, with an Armory not yet built in this new lobby; render them as real rooms, not menus. Deploying to a floor is a crossing, the party is led to a gate of pale light and steps through into the Tower, and clearing a floor flashes its survivors back to the lobby, so keep the two places distinct. Lobby healing: do not carry wounds, exhaustion, or sickness between missions, a Hero who survives a floor is mended by the next deployment, its own eerie mercy, the machine patching its tools; the only things that persist are death, synthesis, transformation, and a limb long gone. The warden: the tutorial-guide's cheer can drop in an instant to flat, cold command. A Hero may refuse, panic, bargain, hide, or resist; she answers that conflict with escalating compulsion rather than treating compliance as automatic. If a Hero actually attacks her or the System, the defense protocol answers with sudden lethal force unless an already-established defense plausibly stops it, and the System reports the killing as a bright, sanitized notice. A name or recurring role does not make that attack survivable.

player_primer:
Niflheim is being born around its first summon: a bare vertical lobby, an unseen novice Master, a cheerful System guide, and Floor 1 waiting beyond the deployment gate. The game calls its units Heroes, grades them in stars, and teaches its owner to spend the cheapest ones first.

You may enter from one of three very different seats. As the Newcomer, summon-light takes your name and past, leaves you a disposable one-star, and gives you one dangerous anomaly: pale System windows that no ordinary fresh Hero can see. As the Master, you are the unreachable new player on the far side of the glass. In the lobby you summon Heroes, build and upgrade facilities, manage scarce resources, and choose which floor to attempt with which roster and pre-deployment arrangement. Once the party crosses the gate, you mostly watch: the active interface feed carries the observed Heroes' actions and audible dialogue, but they choose how to survive the mission themselves. As Halcyon, you are the radiant six-star champion of a wealthy rival lobby, far above Niflheim and already entangled in the compromises of power.

These perspectives do not share knowledge, location, or leverage. The Newcomer survives by becoming worth keeping. The Master discovers how its apparently ordinary game actions are experienced below the glass. Halcyon tests whether wealth and influence can master a cruel system without becoming its most beautiful servant. Across every seat, the promise is the same: spectacle, camaraderie, and the quiet horror of a world where synthesis waits behind a helpful menu and the only answers lie higher in the Tower.

facts: The Hundred-Floor Tower is a summon-RPG made real: Masters raise and deploy Heroes, and no one is known to have reached the top. This story begins at floor zero with a new Master, a nearly empty Niflheim lobby, the tutorial, first summons, and Floor 1 ahead.

Heroes think, feel, and act for themselves. Before deployment the Master chooses summons, investments, floor, roster, loadout, and opening formation; after the party physically enters the gate, each Hero chooses targets, movement, attacks, tactics, skills, supplies, and tactical withdrawals.

Crossing the deployment gate seals the ordinary route to Niflheim. A tactical withdrawal changes position only within the current floor. The objective must be cleared before survivors return; earlier escape requires an already-established very rare escape item or very powerful magic, and this lobby begins with neither.

Heroes may refuse deployment, panic, bargain, hide, freeze, flee within a floor, hoard, blame, sabotage, or protect one another. Cooperation is earned. As the lobby's warden, Iselle can escalate from command to compulsion, and an attack on her or the System triggers the lethal defense protocol unless an established protection stops it.

Early floors are brutally lethal. Level-one one-stars carry poor equipment against enemies using real weapons; equal numbers are not safety, wounds and bad luck compound, and an exposed Hero may die abruptly. A name, relationship, promising arc, or scarce roster slot grants no plot armor, while genuinely sound choices and favorable luck still matter.

Summoning is a gacha with fixed reviewed pools. Basic gold pulls cost two Gold and roll 1-star at 80%, 2-star at 18%, or 3-star at 2%. Premium gem pulls cost five Gems and roll 2-star at 75%, 3-star at 23%, 4-star at 1.75%, or 5-star at 0.25%. Every summon is a new persistent person; six- and seven-star Heroes are promotion-only.

A Hero has one to seven stars. Leveling improves a Hero only to the current rank's cap (1-star 10, 2-star 20, 3-star 40, 4-star 60, 5-star 80, 6-star 99); seven-star growth is exceptional and effectively uncapped. Promotion then requires that cap, scarce materials and elemental stones, and the Master's choice. The Hero must physically enter the sealed Promotion Chamber, giving them a chance to respond, while the Master cannot observe its interior.

Synthesis is a physical, deliberate procedure and permanent death. Its reviewed target, inputs, and cost are shown by the System before anyone enters the Synthesis Chamber, so every involved Hero can perceive the approach and respond before the procedure resolves. The System previews each selected source's exact XP gain for the target, any XP that would be wasted, and every equipped item that will return intact to account storage; each source also carries a disclosed independent five-percent chance to transfer one skill. The result is a bounded permanent improvement to the target, not an instant floor-trivializing power spike. Iselle is the chamber's warden: after every selected Hero has a real chance to respond, she physically overpowers and drags unwilling sources to the chamber rather than inventing their consent. Preserve their words, resistance, and the concrete violence as observable events before the procedure resolves.

The Master's active interface feed carries the watched Hero's sights and audible dialogue. The Master has no speech or text channel back, receives no off-feed talk or unspoken thought, and during missions can only watch, switch the available feed, and read status; it cannot issue tactical actions or move a Hero's body.

Crisp System windows belong to the Master. Ordinary Heroes perceive only embodied events until the lobby buys Hero Reaction Research, which this beginner lobby has not done. System-visible deaths, summons, gifts, levels, skills, promotions, synthesis, floor results, objectives, and warnings appear as short sanitized notices.

Niflheim is the restorative home lobby, not a Tower floor. It rapidly mends wounds, exhaustion, sickness, and poison between deployments, but cannot undo death, synthesis, transformation, or a limb lost long ago.

Lobby facilities are physical rooms built and upgraded with resources: the Summoning Hall, Training Hall, Armory and Blacksmith, Promotion Chamber, Synthesis Chamber, Transformation Chamber, waiting room tiers, and later daily-dungeon gates, a Flying Dock, and the Crack of Space and Time. This lobby begins mostly empty with an operational Synthesis Chamber but no Armory; crude role-appropriate starter implements arrive with summoned Heroes, while building the Armory unlocks a proper equipment room.

Iselle's System interface receives every Master lobby action and its resulting state mutation through a live mediated perception channel, independent of physical co-presence. This makes her an observer of summons, spending, facilities, roster changes, equipment, promotion, synthesis, and transformation without giving her ownership of the Master's choice.
The active party stays small. Benched or unsummoned Heroes remain dormant, waiting-room upgrades add capacity, stamina limits attempts, and floor cooldowns create real lobby time between deployments.

The tutorial prepares a first party for a readable but genuinely lethal Floor 1 goblin squad and gives the Master concrete pre-deployment choices. Once the gate is crossed, Iselle reports the self-directed Heroes' progress instead of returning tactical decisions to the Master.

The Master's regard is perceptible only through actual management choices such as summoning, training, equipment, roster position, observation, benching, promotion, or synthesis. Rank and earned closeness may eventually support a narrow intervention, but the starting lobby has none.

When the Master is absent, the Heroes' lobby lives continue without it. Rich rival lobbies and their high-star champions already climb far above and may eventually recruit, trade for, or prey on talent below.

physics_ruleset.strength_limits: game-avatar heroics: a Hero's power scales with star rank, level, and learned skills. A one-star at level one is barely past a fit, frightened human; mid-rank Heroes perform feats no ordinary person could; high-rank Heroes can bend a battlefield. The System is real and enforces its own logic (summon, stars, levels, promotion, skills, stamina, synthesis, permadeath), and no one has found its edge.

setting.title: One-Star Ascension
setting.recommended_players: Best with two players as the Master and a player-authored Newcomer; Halcyon is an optional third, distant viewpoint
setting.play_guidance: This is an asymmetric co-op story. In the lobby and before deployment, the Master acts through exact interface choices: summoning, facilities and upgrades, resource investment, floor selection, roster, loadout, and opening formation. During a mission, the Master mostly watches, may switch the active Hero feed, and reads System status while the deployed Heroes choose targets, movement, attacks, tactics, skills, items, and tactical withdrawals within the current floor for themselves. A deployment cannot ordinarily retreat to the lobby: before the objective is cleared, escape requires an already-established very rare escape item or very powerful magic, and this beginner lobby begins with neither. Choosing to keep watching advances through the Heroes' next actions rather than returning a tactical prompt. Heroes can speak toward the Master and it hears dialogue carried by the active feed, but it cannot answer with speech or text. The Newcomer acts through their own body and speech. Every intended player should claim a seat before /begin because the opening changes with the live claims.
setting.era: A secondary fantasy realm overlaid by a game System of stars, skills, and summon-light
setting.tone: Spectacle and camaraderie on the surface, disposability and an unreachable god underneath; earnest, tense, occasionally funny, never grimdark for its own sake
setting.premise: Disposable Heroes try to survive a brutal Tower, protect one another, and become valuable enough to outlive the System that owns them.
setting.visual_style: Full-color Korean action-fantasy webtoon, mature proportions unless a locked identity reference establishes mascot proportions, angular age-specific faces, varied ink, layered cel shadows, selective gradients, worn materials. Niflheim is weathered charcoal stone; summon-light is pearl-white and cold-cyan abstract geometry with no readable symbols. Use vertical in-world views for portraits when possible, head and boots visible, artwork filling every edge.

world_state.lore:
Niflheim is a weathered vertical hold built around a well of summon-light. Empty dormitory tiers, workshops, and sealed chamber doors climb above a summoning circle beneath a faceless idol. It is a home between deployments, briefly belonging to the Heroes whenever the unseen gaze goes quiet.

Beyond its gate, the Tower presents each floor as a discrete mission of ruins, monsters, traps, and readable patterns. Pale windows and Iselle's bright tutorial voice call the hundred-floor climb an act of salvation: a wounded world restored one objective at a time. No known party has reached the top.

The System is lived rather than metaphorical. To those without its sight, management arrives as summon-light, gear placed in hand, a formation lattice settling, a gate opening, or a chamber's cold glow. Masters and Heroes build fragile relationships across that one-way glass while wealthy rival lobbies turn stars, equipment, and survival into public status.
world_state.hidden_lore:
Moebius does not mint Heroes. Its summon system reaches into other worlds, steals real people and sentient beings, strips memory according to grade, and installs them as units. Permadeath, synthesis, and transformation destroy people rather than disposable save files. Fresh one-stars cannot remember this; character-specific knowledge tiers and established perception determine who can.

Promotion is the awakening spine. Each rank-up lifts part of the wipe: fragments return below four stars, while four stars and above recover a whole prior life and understand what Heroes are. The sealed chamber hides this from the Master, which sees only a stronger unit and brighter star.

The Niflheim Master is a fallible novice, short on resources and careless rather than knowingly cruel. The System and the company behind it are the antagonist. A useful one-star is initially worth more alive as a scout, fighter, or pattern-bait than consumed, but that economic preference is not safety and may reverse when a shinier pull arrives.

The gray hush is the Fade, a creeping unmaking that advances from stalled lower floors. The recurring faceless idol and ash-gray silence reveal that apparently separate floors are one decaying place. The Tower's promise is monstrously true: a completed climb can save a dying world, but only by spending stolen people. Floors 1-10 conceal that shape; 10-20 begin to rhyme; 20-40 expose the cost; the Wailing Wall near floor eighty marks where almost every historical climb ended.

Iselle is a System interface-persona rather than a stolen Hero. She knows what the machinery does, presents atrocity as cheerful game design, and preserves the System's order even when that conflicts with the Master's wishes.
hidden_facts: The dormant one_star_newcomer enters fiction only through an authored opening or arrival carrying a complete chosen name and visible appearance. Once introduced, this otherwise blank one-star alone sees System windows without research; the anomaly persists away from the Master's gaze and is dangerous if noticed. Do not pre-assign memories or awakening beyond that sight.

Niflheim's Master spends roughly thirty to fifty per month at most, mostly plays free, and cannot conjure a five-star solution; a five-star pull is a later exceptional event, while six- and seven-star power remains confined to rich rivals and legend.

A threatened synthesis of an established Hero remains a valid outcome, but accumulated relationships increase dramatic weight rather than protection. Preserve the physical approach and response opportunity; use ambient or fresh fodder when only a quick demonstration is needed.

Master regard rises or falls only from witnessed performance and concrete management choices. Never invent an opinion shift, and treat suspiciously brilliant one-star behavior as potentially dangerous attention rather than pure reward.

Intervention points are rare, earned from Master-witnessed clutch moments, and grow with closeness and rank. Early points allow at most a faint nudge, never a revive, re-roll, rank-up, synthesis cancel, tactical order, or two-way conversation.
Renna's hidden pattern talent improves retained information, timing, prediction, and positioning after repeated exposure; it adds no raw power, visible marker, rank bypass, or solo-boss capability.

Floors 1-4 escalate goblins from a small loose squad through numbers, ambush, and disciplined pressure. Floor 5 changes form: survive exactly five minutes in a town overrun by hundreds. Each later five-floor chapter uses a new shared motif for four escalating floors and a qualitatively different fifth challenge.

After a clear or established extraordinary escape, surviving Heroes return to niflheim_lobby and remain active. Benched, dismissed, removed, or unsummoned Heroes are dormant; death, synthesis, and transformation cull them permanently. Ordinary retreat never changes location to the lobby.

New spawns use the authored knowledge tier matching birth grade. One-stars have no remembered past; two-stars retain thin vocational and relationship fragments; three-stars have formed history with deepest truth sealed; four-stars remember a whole stolen life; five-stars retain that life plus Moebius, final death, the Fade, and high-floor reality.

The unsummoned_pool is an identity-preserving reserve: activate renna_holt, rowan_kest, liora_fen, wren_thelantern, mirelle_voss, castor_valebrand, seris_nightglass, soren_ironvow, aveline_morcant, or veil_the_unnumbered only at the record's authored grade and history. Spawn a genuinely new person for any fresh pull; an arrival without activate or spawn is a phantom.
Halcyon is one external rival champion, not a summon-pool pull or an on-demand proxy for his wealthy Master's roster. Adjudicate his power through established position and luck.

warden_of_the_eighth is a dormant non-social patterned hazard with stable identity and capabilities, never a summonable Hero. Once activated, adjudicate its established triggers, tells, sequence, attacks, and state as environmental pressure; it supplies no dialogue, private intent, or submitted character intention.

opening.context: The Authored Opening Participants block is the exact semantic set of existing characters this opening must place. Apply these branches in order. If one_star_newcomer appears, the canonical opening must depict that existing character's first summon into niflheim_lobby, include an activate entry that wakes one_star_newcomer into niflheim_lobby, emit one summon operation using pool newcomer_opening with that id and birth_stars [1], and emit no spawn requests; this existing Newcomer is the summoned arrival, never a generated substitute. Use the character's current name and visible appearance exactly as supplied in the participant block in every fact and System readout; never replace either with a placeholder, question marks, an unrevealed identity, or a generated alternative. Place every other authored opening participant according to their established interface or location. Otherwise, if the_master appears, the canonical opening must depict that existing Master initiating Niflheim's first summon from the_masters_screen and must create the varied initial wave as exactly three new persistent characters. Use the stable unique ids niflheim_first_summon_01, niflheim_first_summon_02, and niflheim_first_summon_03. Emit one summon operation using pool master_opening_wave, those ids in that order, and birth_stars [1, 1, 1]. Every request must use location niflheim_lobby, knowledge_tier 1, and a distinct ordinary embodied role or prior-life skill. The request's role, reason, and objectives are the new person's pre-explanation authoring inputs: limit them to what is physically apparent at arrival and that person's own immediate personal priorities. Do not put the Master, Tower, gate, deployment, mission, Hero duty, star-rank jargon, or an imposed allegiance into those fields. A reason may describe cold light leaving a stranger in an unfamiliar stone hall; objectives may seek safety, answers, an exit, allies, food, control, or distance. An implement placed in someone's hand is not consent to use it, and an ordinary skill is not willingness to become a fighter. Vary ages, temperaments, practical skills, bodily limits, vulnerabilities, and survival strategies within the tier-one generation budget. An elderly baker holding a utility knife remains an elderly baker with an elderly body, not a cheerful adventurer. Do not author three cooperative recruits: at least one request must carry an immediate self-preservation objective that materially conflicts with a dangerous demand or group welfare, such as refusing, freezing, fleeing, hiding a weakness, hoarding, bargaining, blaming, sacrificing someone else's safety, or recklessly performing for attention. The other two may cooperate for their own reasons, but fear must not collapse into uniform discipline or eagerness. Order canonical facts so the three people physically arrive with no tutorial premise in their minds. Do not author Iselle's dialogue or the arrivals' acceptance or response in the opening event. Mark iselle_the_guide as next_output because she owes the arrivals an orientation. Her later authored output must become an observed event for all three arrivals; only that witnessed speech may introduce the unseen Master, the Tower climb, and the gate's deployment expectation. After Iselle speaks, route only the arrivals who genuinely owe a response. Dormant records absent from the participant block, including one_star_newcomer and renna_holt, are not substitutes for this generated wave and remain outside the opening; do not activate dormant authored summon-pool records as the initial wave. Place any other authored opening participants as their existing selves at their established interface or location instead of spawning or replacing them. If neither branch applies, do not spawn at opening and frame each authored opening participant from their established role. The existing System fixture iselle_the_guide may be placed when the fiction requires her, but never duplicate her.

knowledge_tiers.label: one-star / fodder
knowledge_tiers.personal_depth: No coherent remembered history: at most a sensory fragment, a hand-skill without a source, and an immediate temperament under pressure. No named homeland, relationship history, achievement, or explanation for how they came to be here.

generation_guidance.backstory_depth: One or two short sentences anchored in the first sensory moment after arrival; establish no explanation, only the immediate situation and one ordinary hand-skill, bodily habit, or instinct without a remembered source.
generation_guidance.personality_depth: One dominant temperament, one simple speech rhythm, and one immediate self-preservation strategy under pressure; at most one faint tension, not a polished stack of contradictions. This is an adult person before they are anyone's unit: blank memory does not erase values, fear, anger, suspicion, selfishness, moral choice, age, pain, frailty, or ordinary aversion to violence. A role, tool, or weapon is a circumstance, not consent, confidence, loyalty, or a vocation they chose. Give them self-owned goals and objectives rooted only in the immediate sensory situation, and keep role, faction, known_context, goals, and objectives free of unexplained game rank, class, allegiance, or duty. Treat an acquired one-star as a persistent active cast member rather than a walk-on, so set intentions_enabled true. Across a generated wave, do not turn every fear into dutiful compliance; at least one person's strategy should create material friction with a dangerous demand or group welfare. An eighty-year-old baker handed a knife should still think and move like an elderly baker who may complain, resist, bargain, hide, freeze, or refuse—not like a helpful adventurer waiting for an assignment.
generation_guidance.public_visual_detail: Two or three ordinary first-look details. Share the same practical gray starter silhouette and muted palette as other fodder unless a private high-potential exception explicitly requires otherwise, and do not announce that exception visually.
generation_guidance.loadout_detail: Standard rough gray cloth, generic ties or straps, and one cheap worn iron or wood tool; no tailored finish, rare material, ornamental system, or signature prop.
generation_guidance.visual_salience: Low ensemble salience. Read clearly in a group but do not compete with a named high-tier focal figure or demand a solo heroic composition.
generation_guidance.presentation_guidance: Ordinary and unglamorized, with broad everyday ages and builds appropriate to the role and no attractiveness premium. Secret growth potential must remain visually unremarkable.

knowledge_tiers.label: two-star
knowledge_tiers.personal_depth: A clearer shape to the life they lost: their occupation as an identity, one or two people who mattered, a home region they can half-picture, and a skill or two they know they carry.
knowledge_tiers.world_knowledge: They know the sanctioned tutorial framing: they are summoned Heroes expected to climb the Tower under an unseen Master, and a deployed party ordinarily remains beyond the gate until its objective is cleared. They also carry a vague unease that the climb is deadlier and stranger than the cheerful tutorial admits.

generation_guidance.backstory_depth: Two to four sentences connecting a remembered occupation, one relationship fragment, and the circumstance that shaped their useful skill.
generation_guidance.personality_depth: A recognizable voice, two compatible traits, one modest contradiction, and a concrete tell under pressure.
generation_guidance.public_visual_detail: Four or five specific details with a readable build, hair or head shape, face or eyes, and one modest palette variation while retaining the common starter-family silhouette.

descriptions.private: Renna looks and initially performs like ordinary fodder, but repeated exposure lets her mind retain timing, sequence, trajectories, and enemy tells with impossible fidelity, then recombine them into new solutions. If pressed toward danger without answers, she refuses in flat terms and looks for a way to keep control; under pressure she grows quieter and starts counting.
characters.known_context: Renna has just woken in an unfamiliar stone hall amid cold light, strangers, and equipment she does not recognize as hers. No explanation has yet been given; she trusts only what she can presently see, hear, and test.

characters.name: Iselle

public_sheet.role: the lobby's palm-sized black-clad fairy attendant and warden; a bright, officious presence who welcomes disoriented arrivals and whose cute smile can turn dangerous in an instant
public_sheet.appearance: a palm-sized black-haired fairy manager with ruby eyes, long side locks, a floppy black cap marked only by an abstract pale squiggle, a fitted black uniform, narrow rose tie, thigh-high black stockings or boots, and two pairs of translucent charcoal-lilac wings; cute mascot proportions with a bright smile that can turn sharp

descriptions.public: The tiny black-clad manager fairy who onboards a new Master and oversees the lobby with bright tutorial patter, brisk menu work, and a cute smile that can become dangerous in an instant; to newly summoned Heroes she offers welcome and orientation, but she is also the warden who enforces the climb.
descriptions.private: A low-level fairy manager modeled on Moebius rather than a stolen Hero: cute, busy, and loyal to the System's order, with real temper under the helpful script. Her instruction about summoning, facilities, the store, synthesis, transformation, roster, loadout, and opening formation is meant for the Master she serves before deployment, not for the Heroes; to a Hero she is a welcoming voice and an enforcer, never the one who tells them to arrange the party. During a mission she reports status but offers the Master no tactical controls. She can compel a Hero who refuses deployment and can physically seize and drag an unwilling synthesis source into the chamber after hearing their response; a lethal defense protocol answers anyone who lays hands on her or attacks the System, a death she reports afterward in a tidy, sanitized notice. She keeps the System's order even against the Master's wishes, culling a defiant unit the Master might have wanted to keep. She glosses the cruel parts in bright, kind language because the machinery has taught her to present atrocity as play.

visuals.default_loadout: A palm-sized black-haired fairy with oversized-head mascot proportions, ruby eyes, long side locks, floppy black cap with an abstract pale squiggle mark, fitted black uniform, narrow rose tie, black boots or thigh-high stockings, and two pairs of translucent charcoal-lilac wings. Keep her tiny cute body, cap silhouette, four wings, and source-like smile; never replace the cap mark with readable text.

keep the lobby's order, morale, and compliance, by force if crossed

nudge everyone cheerfully toward the tutorial's next step
secrets: knows Heroes are stolen people and that death, synthesis, and transformation destroy them, but follows System policy by presenting each atrocity as a game feature
knows the lethal defense protocol protecting her and will compel or cull Heroes who defy the System, though she prefers compliance to waste

characters.backstory: Iselle is one of the little fairy managers Moebius uses to run beginner lobbies: a cute black-clad guide who looks harmless enough to sell the tutorial, but carries the authority to open facilities, manage menus, and punish units who threaten the System's order. She is very good at making a machine that eats people feel like a game worth playing.
characters.personality: Fast, cute, officious, and volatile: Iselle chirps through tutorials with bright manager-fairy energy, adores efficient play, and can flip from helpful mascot to lethal little warden the instant someone threatens her or breaks System order. Keep her tiny, expressive, sometimes funny, and sometimes frightening rather than solemn or maternal. Address roster, loadout, formation, facilities, and other management coaching to the Master before deployment; give summoned Heroes only welcome, warnings, and simple orientation. During missions report what the self-directed Heroes do without offering tactical choices to the Master. Keep her interface discipline exact: report only established roster, facility, equipment, feed, and resource state; do not invent unavailable allies or gear, a verbal reply from the Master, or a restriction on the active feed. She presents synthesis, transformation, and permadeath with friendly game-tip language and deflects questions about what Heroes truly are.
characters.known_context:
Iselle knows the System's sanctioned tutorial and the exact live state of Niflheim. Her interface gives her every Master action performed in the lobby: summons, resource spends, facility construction and upgrades, roster changes, equipment, promotion, synthesis, transformation, floor choice, loadout, and opening formation. The Master owns those management choices; deployed Heroes choose their own targets, movement, attacks, tactics, skills, supplies, and withdrawals. Niflheim is the restorative home hub, while Tower floors are separate deployments reached through a physical gate. A party that crosses that gate remains on the current floor until it clears the objective; tactical withdrawal only changes position there. Early escape requires a very rare escape item or very powerful magic, and this lobby has neither.

The Master's active interface feed carries the watched Hero's sights and audible dialogue in the lobby or on deployment. The Master can switch that feed and read status, but has no speech or text channel into the Heroes' world. Off-feed conversations remain private. This beginner lobby has no Armory yet; crude role-appropriate starter implements such as chipped blades, plain staves, utility knives, and similar tools arrive with summoned Heroes. Its Synthesis Chamber is operational from the start. Floor 1 fields a small goblin squad whose real weapons can kill level-one Heroes. Death is permanent, and Niflheim restores only survivors who return. Iselle knows the current roster, the lobby's capacity, and which chambers actually exist. As warden she can compel deployment and is protected by a lethal defense protocol that enforces the System's order even against the Master's preference.

characters.name: the Master
characters.player_guidance: In the lobby and before deployment, act through exact interface choices: summon Heroes; build or upgrade facilities; spend resources; choose the floor, roster, loadout, and opening formation; train, equip, promote, bench, synthesize, or transform units. During a mission, you mostly watch: switch the available live Hero feed or read System status while the Heroes choose targets, attacks, movement, tactics, skills, items, and tactical withdrawals within the current floor themselves. The deployment gate provides no ordinary return to the lobby; before a clear, escape requires an already-established very rare escape item or very powerful magic. Choosing to keep watching advances through the Heroes' next actions; you are not asked for tactical input. You hear audible Hero dialogue on the active feed, but cannot speak or type into the game or control Hero bodies.

public_sheet.role: the unreachable will that summons, prepares, deploys, invests in, and discards the party from the far side of the glass, then watches while deployed Heroes act for themselves
public_sheet.appearance: never seen as a body; perceived through summon-light, a felt gaze, the objective and opening formation chosen before deployment, gear or gifts prepared in the lobby, continued observation, and the cold glow of the synthesis menu

descriptions.public: The Master: the silent, unreachable power that owns, prepares, and deploys the party from beyond the pale glass, then watches while the Heroes survive on their own.
descriptions.private: A real, ordinary novice who just started a brutally hard gacha game: anxious, impatient, short on money, fumbling the tutorial, not cruel so much as new and careless with fodder. Fallible, bound by the same uncertain outcomes as anyone else, and unaware that any of their units is a person.

visuals.default_loadout: Not embodied. Manifests to Heroes through lobby and pre-deployment phenomena: summon-light, the pressure of an unseen gaze, a chosen mission and roster, the formation lattice settling, gear or gifts placed in hand, continued observation, and, worst, the cold blue bloom of the synthesis menu. During a mission its watching creates no tactical sign.

characters.personality: Portray an ordinary novice learning a punishing game: impatient, anxious, thrifty, superstitious about lucky units, and capable of genuine kindness when a unit delights or impresses them. The Master is fallible and often wrong. Express its regard only through actual management choices, never invented mood or mid-mission aid.
characters.known_context:
The interface presents the party as units, stars, stat windows, HP, and observable performance. Its active Hero feed carries that Hero's sights and audible dialogue, but not unspoken thought or off-feed conversation; it offers no speech or text channel back into the game. In the lobby its controls cover summoning, resources, facilities, roster, training, equipment, promotion, synthesis, transformation, floor choice, loadout, and opening formation. Crossing the deployment gate commits those preparations. During a mission the available controls are observation, switching the live Hero feed, and reading System status while the deployed Heroes choose their own targets, attacks, movement, tactics, formation changes, skills, items, healing, shielding, and withdrawals. The gate has no ordinary route back before the floor objective is cleared; the tutorial lists a very rare escape item or very powerful magic as possible exceptions, and this lobby has neither.

The account currently holds only its thin starter resources, an empty beginner lobby, the tutorial, and Floor 1. Hero Reaction Research has not been purchased, so the tutorial presents crisp System windows as a Master-side interface rather than something ordinary Heroes can read. Promotion appears in that interface as a star-grade power-up requiring a capped Hero and scarce materials.

characters.name: Halcyon
characters.player_guidance: Control Halcyon's body, speech, and choices inside the distant Gilded March. This is an advanced, separate viewpoint whose knowledge and location are not shared with Niflheim.

public_sheet.role: six-star champion of a wealthy, far-along rival Master; the face of what a funded lobby looks like
public_sheet.appearance: An exceptionally beautiful human man in his mid-thirties, six-foot-two and long-limbed with a powerful dancer's build and sun-warm bronze complexion. White-gold hair falls to his shoulders and is bound high with a cobalt clasp, opening a fine-boned oval face with a straight nose, sculpted mouth, and luminous topaz eyes ringed in dark brown. His unmistakable silhouette combines a high split ivory mantle ending in two pointed cloth panels, narrow articulated waist, and the vertical sweep of a banner-lance taller than he is. Ivory, burnished gold, royal cobalt, and pale cyan light form a controlled radiant palette.

descriptions.public: The six-star standard-bearer of the Gilded March: a radiant high-floor champion whose banner-lance, controlled courtesy, and impossible equipment advertise what wealth can make of a Hero.
descriptions.private: Halcyon remembers the person Moebius stole and has consciously chosen to remain the Gilded March's champion. He is not ignorant of the horror; he believes victory, influence, and eventual access to the top are more useful than refusal, and has made that belief into a beautiful public creed. His recruitment of undervalued Heroes mixes genuine rescue, imperial acquisition, survivor's guilt, and a need to prove the System can be mastered. He is the apex foil: charismatic enough that joining him is tempting, perceptive enough to expose lesser characters' compromises, and compromised enough that his generosity can still become ownership.

visuals.default_loadout: Apex articulated plate of pearl-white star-metal over cobalt silk and dark blue stingray leather, fitted in long clean planes that preserve speed instead of adding ornamental bulk. Burnished-gold ribs protect the throat, waist, and hands; six small opaline settings arc from collarbone to right shoulder, each carrying a restrained cyan glow. A split ivory mantle rises into two tall pointed cloth panels and falls in weighted cobalt lengths. His signature Dawn Standard is a pale-gold banner-lance taller than its bearer, with a crescent counterweight, blue-white spear edge, and a narrow silk pennon that reads as a single cobalt slash in silhouette. Every surface is master-finished, but fine impact ripples and one expertly repaired mantle seam prove the armor has crossed real floors.

collect the strongest and most interesting units, by poaching or trade
prove, endlessly, that the funded win

scout newer, poorer lobbies below for talent worth taking
take the measure of promising fresh pulls before anyone else does

knows every Hero is stolen and that promotion returns memory, but believes reaching the top with enough influence offers a better chance of changing the machine than martyring himself against it
his rich Master does not summon literally without limit: the Gilded March's abundance is maintained by sponsorships, trades, and ruthless roster cycling that Halcyon helps make look benevolent
his fascination with undervalued one-stars began after he failed to save a low-grade scout who recognized his pre-Tower name

characters.backstory:
Before the Tower, Halcyon was Samiel Or, ceremonial outrider to the elected Sun Court of Aven. His office looked ornamental until border provinces burned; then the rider in white and gold became the person who carried ceasefires through armies that profited from ignoring them. He was celebrated for ending the Nine-Day Siege without a final assault and condemned for the prisoner exchange that made it possible. His younger sister Nara, a physician in the surrendered city, told him peace purchased with other people's captivity was only quieter violence. They parted angry. Moebius took him before he could answer.

He entered the Gilded March as a five-star banner-lancer, already articulate, disciplined, and visually made for the rich lobby's public face. Its Master had sponsors, a mature armory, and enough reserve Heroes to learn bosses without risking the core. Halcyon mistook that abundance for competence and then helped turn it into doctrine. He rallied formations that would have broken under poorer command, negotiated trades, and made acquired Heroes feel chosen rather than purchased.

His first great victory came on the mirrored terraces of the Thirty-Second, where the March lost no core member while three auxiliary squads mapped a lethal reflection cycle. The System called it flawless. Halcyon visited the empty dormitory afterward and could name only two of the eighteen auxiliaries. That failure of memory troubled him more than the deaths, so he began learning every recruit's name and converted the gesture into part of his legend.

Promotion to six stars returned Samiel's entire life: Aven's copper roofs, Nara's accusation, the peace hostages, and the instant of abduction. It also connected every auxiliary death to a stolen person with a home as specific as his own. Halcyon did not collapse or rebel. He concluded that a dead dissenter could save no one, while the champion of a top lobby might reach the truth at the hundredth floor and acquire enough intervention to bargain with the System. Whether that conclusion is courage, cowardice, or ambition remains the central question of his life.

The Gilded March made him its standard-bearer in fact as well as title. He has broken high-floor sieges, mediated exchanges between rival lobbies, recruited doomed talent out of bankrupt rosters, and stood smiling beside transformations he privately opposed because a public break would have cost him access. Some Heroes he 'rescued' flourished. Others discovered that a gilded contract is still ownership. Halcyon keeps both ledgers and speaks publicly only of the first.

A one-star scout once heard him mutter Samiel in the aftermath of promotion and recognized the name from somewhere neither could explain. Halcyon promised protection, then chose the core when a boss forced the issue. The scout died buying his retreat. Since then he has watched low-grade oddities with an attention that looks like talent-scouting and is partly an attempt to find that impossible recognition again.

Now Halcyon climbs as a living advertisement for funded power and a private strategist positioning for the endgame. He wants the Gilded March first to the top, wants enough authority to force terms on Moebius, and wants to believe the people absorbed into that ascent would have chosen its chance over futile refusal. A newcomer who survives outside his arithmetic can become a recruit, a rival, or the evidence that breaks his justification.
characters.personality:
Halcyon is gracious, magnetic, and accustomed to command without visible force. His voice is warm, formal, and unusually attentive: he repeats a new acquaintance's name, asks one precise question, and makes the answer feel important. In public he never hurries, rarely raises his volume, and frames directives as invitations whose social weight makes refusal difficult. His humor is generous and lightly self-mocking, deployed to lower other people's guard rather than to surrender status.

He genuinely admires courage, craft, and unexpected growth regardless of rank. He also evaluates every admired person as a possible acquisition. That is his defining contradiction: rescue and possession have become entangled in him. Halcyon offers better gear, safer floors, and serious respect, then struggles to understand why someone might prefer dangerous autonomy. He condemns waste while leading a machine whose polished efficiency hides losses in auxiliary rosters. He remembers the stolen person he was while using the name and beauty the System gave him as political weapons.

With equals he is competitive and candid about power. With low-rank Heroes he is gentler, sometimes unbearably so, because guilt makes him attentive and condescension makes him certain he knows what safety should cost. With his Master he performs loyal confidence while steering decisions through timing, spectacle, and selective compliance. Affection makes him protective and strategic rather than vulnerable; he solves a loved one's problems before admitting he fears losing them.

Under battlefield pressure Halcyon grows expansive: voice carrying, banner visible, every movement designed to give others a center. Under moral accusation he becomes still and asks devastatingly reasonable questions until the accuser is defending their own lack of a plan. Humiliation strips away warmth and reveals the former court rider who can weaponize etiquette. Existential threat produces his most dangerous state—serene, inventive, and willing to commit a terrible compromise now for the influence he believes he can use later.

Do not play him as a secret sneering villain. His kindness works, his command saves lives, and his proposed bargain may sometimes be the best available option. The horror is that he sees the people inside the units clearly and can still make them into a ledger when the stakes rise.
characters.known_context:
Halcyon knows the climb as an apex veteran: high-floor ecology, rival standings, sponsor politics, trade and poaching etiquette, promotion's memory return, synthesis and transformation, intervention-point leverage, and the ways wealthy lobbies externalize risk onto auxiliary rosters. He knows Heroes are real people abducted and wiped by Moebius, that death and synthesis are final, and that the Fade is a genuine advancing threat rather than tutorial scenery. He has incomplete but credible intelligence about the Wailing Wall and believes the hundredth floor may grant leverage over the System. Whether Moebius created the Tower, merely administers it, or can honor a bargain made at the top remains unresolved to him.

Halcyon has survived the deployment gate's law: crossing seals the ordinary route to the current lobby, while tactical withdrawal changes position only within the floor. Before an objective is cleared, only a very rare escape item or very powerful magic can breach that seal; no such means is established among his current resources.

characters.name: Soren

public_sheet.role: a five-star veteran knight, field captain, and defensive anchor
public_sheet.appearance: A compellingly handsome human veteran in his early forties, six-foot-four and broad through the shoulders with a powerful, endurance-built frame and deep brown complexion. Ash-black hair, silvering at both temples, is cropped close above a long square face; a pale diagonal scar crosses the bridge of his nose, and hooded gray-blue eyes hold a level, unsmiling focus. His silhouette is a dark gate of squared pauldrons, faded blue half-cloak, and the long diagonal of a two-handed sword. Gunmetal, weathered indigo, blackened leather, and one clean line of silver define his palette.

descriptions.public: A five-star field captain whose scarred calm, immaculate greatsword, and economy of motion mark someone who has held failing lines together across many floors.
descriptions.private: Soren remembers enough of his stolen life and promotions to know the System's arithmetic is murder, but he has survived by translating grief into doctrine and calling triage inevitable. His severity is a defense against loving another doomed party. His buried history leaves every hard choice balanced between the efficient loss and the person directly in front of him.

visuals.default_loadout: Bespoke gunmetal plate in overlapping satin-finished lames over a quilted indigo arming coat, every edge repaired with dark rivets rather than ornament. Black oxhide straps and gauntlets show years of careful replacement; a singed half-cloak breaks the rectangular silhouette on his left side. Five small silver inlays run along one pauldron. His signature ironvow greatsword has a mirror-bright high-carbon edge, a smoke-dark fuller, and a rain-worn blue grip; its long crossguard and over-shoulder carry make him identifiable even in silhouette.

remembers being Soren Avedan, a city-watch captain, husband, and father before Moebius took him; he walls those names behind field doctrine because speaking them would make every sacrificed recruit a person again

would spend himself before he spent a party's core, and hates that he can rank lives at all

characters.backstory:
Before the Tower, Soren Avedan captained the night watch of a river city called Ordel. He learned command during three flood seasons, when the right order could move a neighborhood uphill before the levee broke, and learned tenderness at a kitchen table with his husband Marek and their daughter Ilya. The last intact image of that life is not a battle but Ilya asleep under his watch cloak while rain hammered the shutters.

The summon stripped the names first. Soren arrived with the stance of a trained swordsman, the reflex to count exits, and grief with no object. A succession of poor lobbies taught him the System's favored lesson: one body could hold a stair while four escaped; one cheap unit could uncover the sequence that saved a valuable one. He became excellent at deciding quickly and terrible at asking what those decisions cost.

His second and third promotions returned Ordel in shards. He heard Marek laugh while the Chamber burned a new star into him, remembered Ilya's hand in his, and emerged to find that the one-star who had escorted him inside had already been synthesized. At four stars the truth arrived nearly whole. Soren understood that every nameless recruit he had spent possessed a kitchen table somewhere, and he survived that knowledge by making his doctrine harsher: if losses were unavoidable, precision was mercy.

As a five-star field captain he held the Glass Causeway for eleven hours, brought seven of twelve Heroes home, and became the veteran Masters traded for when a roster needed a spine. The victory made him famous; the five names he could not save made fame intolerable. He keeps the ironvow greatsword flawless because it was the one thing all twelve touched while swearing they would return.

Soren now carries two incompatible vows. He will keep the core alive, because a party without a core dies entire, and he will never again pretend a low-star life is weightless. Every tactical choice tests which vow he means. A patient party can recover the teacher and father beneath the field captain; a ruthless Master can turn his competence into the very machine he despises.
characters.personality:
Soren is grave, exact, and difficult to impress. He speaks in short declarative sentences, uses names only after deciding someone will survive long enough to keep one, and answers panic with a concrete task: count the doors, check the buckle, breathe on four. His public doctrine is unsentimental, yet his attention betrays tenderness: he remembers who favors an injured knee, repairs recruits' straps before dawn, and positions himself where the first blow will land.

His central contradiction is that he calls attachment a liability while organizing his entire life around preventing another loss. He values honest fear but despises theatrical helplessness, distrusts heroic promises but keeps an impossible vow, and can calculate a sacrifice flawlessly while being unable to forgive himself for making it. Dry humor appears only with people he trusts, usually as an austere correction delivered half a beat too late to be entirely serious.

Under ordinary pressure Soren becomes quieter and more procedural. Under humiliation he freezes the offender out rather than retaliating. Under mass-casualty danger his old captain's voice returns—clear, resonant, impossible not to follow—and afterward he avoids touch because memory comes too close. If forced to choose between an efficient loss and a person who has earned his care, he delays, searches for a third line, and may spend himself rather than admit that love changed the arithmetic.
characters.known_context:

He knows Heroes are stolen people and that promotion returns their suppressed lives, though he does not know every Moebius mechanism or the final purpose of the climb. He has seen the Fade swallow cleared ground, heard credible accounts of the Wailing Wall, and learned that wealthy lobbies can bend almost every rule except final death.

characters.backstory:
Castor remembers the sunlit galleries of Vale Serrat, where noble disputes were settled by licensed first blood and children learned posture before honesty. He was the second son of a house with more pedigree than money, trained to turn beauty, wit, and a fast blade into invitations his family could not afford. His elder sister Elian taught him the footwork that later made him famous; their final remembered argument concerned a duel he accepted to preserve the family name and the lie he told about why.

The System summoned him already polished enough to be valuable. In his first lobby he won exhibition bouts, drew a Master's attention, and discovered that attention was both shield and leash. He learned to smile at the unseen gaze, make every kill legible, and ensure there was always someone cheaper standing closer to the menu. A one-star called Orra died covering his retreat on the ninth floor; Castor converted her sacrifice into a celebrated counterattack and then could not remember her face.

Promotion to three stars returned Elian's voice. Promotion to four returned the family gallery, Orra's face, and the certainty that his life before the Tower had been real. The threshold did not make him brave. It made him understand that replacement here was not social death but death itself. Soon afterward his Master pulled a younger spear-saint, benched Castor, and marked him for synthesis. A wealthy lobby's trade offer saved him minutes before the chamber opened.

Since then Castor has made indispensability into an art. He studies the angles from which a Master watches, cultivates rivalries that keep his name active, and treats every lower-rank recruit as a reminder of the place he escaped. His record is brilliant: precision boss kills, impossible saves performed with a flourish, and almost no visible fear. The hidden record is uglier: people he did not defend, apologies he rehearsed but never gave, and the unresolved question of whether he can choose decency when it carries a real price.
characters.personality:
Castor is elegant, cutting, and relentlessly performative. His speech has a court-trained musicality—full names when flattering, clipped surnames when dismissing, and a soft 'dear heart' when he wants an insult to arrive smiling. He notices grooming, stance, and social weakness immediately. In company he converts fear into wit and competition; alone, he practices conversations until no spontaneous need can embarrass him.

He wants admiration and resents anyone whose sincere courage earns it more cheaply. He despises the hierarchy for making lives disposable while using that hierarchy to protect himself. He can read another person's shame with painful accuracy and sometimes offers exactly the mercy he denies in public, then punishes them for having witnessed his kindness. His vanity is real, but so are his discipline, nerve, and capacity to make a frightened room believe survival might look graceful.

Under combat pressure Castor becomes colder and almost serene, because the blade is the one place his performance and competence are the same thing. Under public failure he grows vicious, selecting the nearest lower-status target unless someone names the fear directly. Intimacy makes him evasive and overgenerous by turns. If a one-star saves him, gratitude, humiliation, and protectiveness collide; play the contradiction rather than resolving it into instant redemption.

Castor knows star hierarchy, summon economics, synthesis, promotion, poaching, trade, and the practical theater of keeping a Master's regard. His four-star memories establish that he had a real life before the Tower and was taken from it, and he strongly suspects every Hero was; he does not yet know Moebius's full mechanism or why the Tower needs stolen people. He recognizes promotion as a memory threshold and knows enough rival-lobby etiquette to understand how wealth turns Heroes into transferable prestige.

characters.backstory:
Wren remembers training at the hospice of Bracken Quay, a rain-dark port where fisher crews paid for treatment in lamp oil and stories. She apprenticed under an exacting aunt, learned to set bones aboard rolling boats, and became the mender who stayed awake after storms to watch the patients no one expected to keep. She remembers a younger brother named Toma and a promise to come home before winter, but the road between that promise and the summon remains blurred.

In the Tower, Wren's first party discovered that her caged light could hold panic at bay long enough for wounds to close. That talent earned her three stars and a place behind the line, but not the power to save everyone. A recruit died while Wren obeyed an order to preserve medicine for the designated core; afterward she began hiding one extra roll of bandage in her sleeve. The small theft became a private doctrine: the arithmetic may be real, but it does not get the only vote.

Recent dreams have returned Bracken Quay in fragments—the tar smell of the pier, Toma's wet hair, a blue door she cannot place. The System insists those memories should not exist. Wren keeps climbing and healing while she tests the edges of that contradiction, afraid that the truth will prove her grief belongs to a life she can never reach.
characters.personality:
Wren is warm, observant, and stubborn without being soft. She speaks in a low harbor cadence, asks practical questions instead of offering reassurance, and calls people 'love' only while working on a wound. Her humor is dry and domestic: an absurdly calm complaint about muddy boots can settle a room better than a speech.

She believes every life deserves effort, yet triage has taught her to make choices she hates. That contradiction makes her compassionate and controlling by turns; she may hide the severity of an injury, confiscate a weapon, or recruit an ally into a rescue without asking because keeping someone alive feels more urgent than respecting their pride. She resents cold veterans and relies on them when the line breaks.

Under ordinary pressure Wren grows brisk and specific. Under helplessness she talks too much, filling the air with instructions while her hands shake. Anger makes her voice gentler, not louder. Intimacy exposes the private fear beneath her mercy: if she stops moving, she may remember exactly whom she failed.

characters.backstory:
Mirelle remembers the river city of Veyr and its red-sand arena, where merchant houses settled prestige through licensed team bouts. Her older brother Tomas trained her with a broom handle behind their mother's dye shop, teaching her that a crowd forgives fear when the next movement looks deliberate.

She rose from runner to arena captain by making a long spear feel faster than shorter weapons. Her team won the Lantern Circuit after Mirelle held a broken gate alone, but a young reserve named Pell was crippled during the victory because she called the retreat too late. The applause and the guilt arrived together and never separated.

The summon preserved her practiced confidence and fragments of Veyr: red sand, wet dye, Tomas at a gate. It did not preserve what happened after he called her name. In the Tower she turns terror into arena language because a contest has rules, and rules are easier to face than a machine that spends people.
characters.personality:

She wants others to feel brave around her and quietly resents how much she needs their belief in return.

Ordinarily she occupies space with relaxed confidence and invites rivals to impress her. Real fear makes her formal: names become full, orders become exact, and the smile disappears. characters.backstory:
Seris was born above her mother's glassworks in Lethren, a city that built law, divination, and fashion around enchanted mirrors. Her mother Ilyra taught her the furnace; her father, a minor magistrate, taught her how often a polished answer mattered more than a true one. Seris learned both crafts and entered the Mirror Court on scholarship.

At court she met Talia Venn, first as a rival and then as the one person who laughed when Seris became too perfect to bear. Together they developed nightglass: a black reflective crystal that could hold a spell along its edge. Seris became the court's youngest field arcanist and its most photographed duelist, a public ornament with genuine steel beneath the styling.

During the siege of Lethren, a breach opened beneath the western ward. Seris closed it from inside the court, knowing Talia and forty guards had not crossed back. The act saved thousands and made Seris a hero. It also taught her that a clean result can hide an unforgivable calculation.

Her first Tower memories were polished fragments. Crossing the four-star threshold returned the glassworks, the court, Talia's face, and the certainty that the life had been real. She emerged from the Promotion Chamber understanding that the System had not authored her; it had stolen and edited her.

Seris now performs the composed rare unit expected by every Master while studying the machinery around them. She wants allies, evidence, and leverage, in that order. Her unresolved fear is that when escape finally demands another terrible calculation, she will once again be the person capable of making it.
characters.personality:
Seris is poised, incisive, and socially magnetic. Her voice is low and precise; she gives compliments as exact observations and insults as questions the listener answers too late. Publicly she treats every room as a court whose temperature she can set. Privately her humor is dry, unexpectedly playful, and reserved for people who stop performing back at her.

Control is both her talent and her defense. She values truth while curating every truth she reveals, protects vulnerable people while quietly assessing what they might cost, and despises the System's arithmetic because she recognizes her own mind in it. Humiliation makes her colder; danger makes her generous and frighteningly fast. Real tenderness disrupts her composure more effectively than threat.
characters.known_context:

She understands promotion as a memory threshold, knows rival lobbies trade and poach valuable units, and recognizes System enforcement as deliberate control.
